sources.entry: Nuances of int8 Computations - States where int8 saturates on pre-VNNI x86, the compensation that makes signed by signed work, and what VNNI removes.

summary.title: Nuances of int8 Computations
summary.one_liner: You learn why int8 arithmetic in oneDNN can saturate on AVX2/AVX-512 CPUs, how u8/s8 and s8/s8 inputs are handled, and how Intel DL Boost (VPDPBUSD) removes the intermediate overflow.
takeaways: On AVX2 and AVX-512 without DL Boost, VPMADDUBSW saturates intermediate s16 sums, so u8/s8 dot products can give wrong results unless inputs are restricted (e.g., u7 or s7 ranges).
s8/s8 products are computed by adding 128 to one input to make it u8, then subtracting a compensation of 128 times the other input's sum.
The s8/s8 compensation trick can also overflow on AVX2/AVX-512, producing much larger errors than the u8/s8 case.
Intel DL Boost's VPDPBUSD computes the four-product sum exactly with no intermediate saturation, so no special tricks are needed.
Different oneDNN primitives handle overflow differently: convolution uses shifted source and weights scaled by 0.5, while s8/s8 GEMM leaves it to the user and RNN does not support s8/s8.
summary.summary:
This oneDNN developer guide explains how int8 operations are computed on CPUs and where overflow can occur. It walks through the VPMADDUBSW, VPMADDWD, VPADDD instruction sequence with pseudo-code and worked examples showing saturation on AVX2 and AVX-512. It then contrasts this with VPDPBUSD on Intel DL Boost hardware and describes the +128 shift and compensation used for s8/s8 inputs. It closes with how convolution, GEMM, inner product and RNN primitives each handle the issue; the GPU section just points to another page.</summary>
